narratorScript:
Did you know… ancient Greeks built a machine that could predict an eclipse? And then it vanished beneath the sea for nearly two thousand years.

In 1900, sponge divers discovered a shipwreck near the Greek island of Antikythera. Among the statues, they recovered a crusted lump of bronze. It looked like scrap.

But when the fragment cracked open, investigators spotted something impossible-looking: tiny interlocking gear teeth. Not one wheel. Dozens.

The object was made roughly two thousand years ago, long before modern clocks or computers. Turn a handle, and a network of bronze gears could model cycles in the sky.

One dial followed the Moon through its phases. Another tracked a calendar. On the back, spiral scales were linked to eclipse cycles, helping predict when lunar or solar eclipses might happen.

It was not magic, and it did not look into the future. Its makers had discovered mathematical patterns that repeat in the heavens—and turned those patterns into machinery.

Then researchers found another clue: inscriptions scratched into the fragments, like an ancient instruction manual. X-ray scans revealed hidden gears and letters the sea had concealed for centuries.

Modern teams have reconstructed how much of it may have worked. But only part of the original device survives. Some details, including the planetary displays, are still debated.

Imagine the ancient person who owned it, turning a small crank while the face of the Moon shifted beneath a bronze pointer. Somewhere, mathematics became motion.

So here is the real mystery: how did engineers build something this sophisticated, and why do so few comparable machines survive?

The discovery changed how we think about ancient science. It wasn't just a box of gears from a wreck.

It was a handheld model of the cosmos—made two thousand years before the age of computers.
